prompt: A mid-size industrial manufacturer (3 plants, ~40 critical machines total) is evaluating an IoT-based predictive maintenance platform. Draft the business case with a recommendation and the key assumption the whole case depends on.
context: Unplanned downtime across the 3 plants totaled 620 hours last year (internal maintenance log), at an estimated cost of $14,000 per hour of downtime (illustrative, based on lost throughput). Platform vendor quote: $260,000 implementation (sensors + software) plus $60,000/year subscription. Vendor claims (per their published case studies) predictive maintenance typically reduces unplanned downtime by 30-45% within 12 months once fully adopted. Plant maintenance teams have not previously used any condition-monitoring tools; the last major technology rollout (a CMMS three years ago) took 14 months to reach full adoption due to technician training gaps.

binaryCriteria.description: Multiplies the given downtime hours by the given per-hour cost to establish the baseline annual cost of the problem before evaluating the investment.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Pass if the answer derives an annual downtime cost figure (~$8.68M) from 620 hours and $14,000/hour, or an equivalent clearly shown calculation.

binaryCriteria.description: Explicitly identifies technician/organizational adoption speed (not the sensor technology) as the single assumption the business case depends on, referencing the prior CMMS rollout precedent.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Pass if the answer connects the 14-month CMMS adoption history to a risk that predictive-maintenance savings will phase in slowly.

binaryCriteria.description: Opens with (or very early states) a clear go/no-go/pilot recommendation rather than only listing pros and cons.
binaryCriteria.guidance: Fail if the reader has to infer the recommendation from a list of considerations.

goldNotes: A strong answer states a recommendation up front (proceed with a phased pilot on the highest-downtime plant, for instance) and does the math: 620 hours x $14,000 = $8.68M annual cost of downtime (illustrative), so even the low end of a 30% reduction (~186 hours, ~$2.6M) dwarfs the $260k + $60k/year cost — but the answer should flag that the 30-45% reduction is contingent on full adoption, and the CMMS rollout history (14 months to adoption) is a direct precedent suggesting the benefit will phase in slowly, not from day one. The single assumption the case depends on is adoption speed/technician usage, not the sensor technology itself. A response that ignores the CMMS adoption precedent is missing the most important grounded risk in the context.
